amendments.rule: **A verbless clause with a prepositional predicate takes its supplied copula on the preposition.** Rule 20 supplies the copula from the construction; where the predicate is a prepositional phrase, the copula joins the preposition heading that phrase and the unit heads on the preposition — `בְכַפֵּיהֶם` → *is in their hands*, `בִמְסִלּוֹתָם` → *are in their paths*, `אִתָּנוּ` → *are with us*, `עָלֶיךָ` → *is upon thee*. **A directional predicate whose relation is carried by a directive `he` rather than by a preposition is read on the same terms.** Rule 32 makes such a `he` its own aligned unit by rule 11 wherever the ASV writes a word of its own for it, so where that directional phrase is the predicate of a verbless clause the construction-supplied copula joins the `he`'s unit and that unit heads on the word written for the direction, discontinuous around the noun under rule 25: `דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה רְאוּבֵן תֵּימָנָה` → *On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben* gives *On … shall be* to the `he`, while `תֵּימָן` keeps *the south side*, headed on *south* under rule 31, and the construct chain keeps only its own English. Read the Hebrew for which side is the predicate, as this rule's closing paragraph and rule 20 both direct: a definite construct chain standing in such a clause is its subject, and the ASV's inversion of the English is not evidence against that. Two limits. Where the ASV writes no separate word for the `he` and the two share one unit under rule 30, there is no separate unit to carry the copula and it joins that one fused unit. And where a participial or other nominal phrase is the clause's subject, so that the directional phrase is not the predicate at all, rule 20 governs and the copula joins the nominal predicate instead — `וְהַחֹנִים קֵדְמָה מִזְרָחָה דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה יְהוּדָה` → *And those that encamp on the east side toward the sunrising shall be they of the standard of the camp of Judah* leaves the directive `he` its bare *on*. **A resultative prepositional predicate takes the ASV's supplied result or change frame on the same terms.** The preposition carries the relation that English expresses with the frame: `לְ` → *to be*, *shall be turned into*, *will be unto*, or *shalt become*. This is not rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb, because removing the English frame removes the preposition's own result relation; any explicit Hebrew subject still takes the English subject pronoun separately. Head the preposition's unit on the English word carrying that relation — *to* in *to be*, *into* in *shall be turned into*, *unto* in *will be unto*, and *become* where no English preposition remains. The ordinary copular case is settled rather than a tie: the corpus reads it this way in 103 units across 39 chapters and never moves the copula onto the object noun instead. It is settled; the note need not hedge it. **A relational verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand goes the same way.** Where a possessive or belonging `לְ` heads the predicate and the ASV renders the clause with a verb of belonging rather than a bare copula — `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which belonged to the house* — that verb is part of the preposition's own rendering and joins its unit, headed on the English preposition written for it. It is not rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb: drop the verb and the preposition's relation is what has gone and nothing else, which is the subtraction test rule 43 applies to the same clause written with *had*. Where the ASV does write *had* or *have*, rule 43 governs; where it writes a bare copula, the first sentence of this rule does. **But every sentence above governs a phrase for which the ASV has written an English preposition, and says nothing about one for which it has written none.** Where the ASV spends no word on the preposition's own relation and instead writes that relation inside the following word — a possessive or belonging `לְ` rendered as an English genitive, `לַיהוָה` → *is Jehovah's* — rule 30's one-rendering condition is met: one English word carries both the relation and the lexeme, and the preposition shares that word's unit, headed on the word carrying the lexeme. The construction's copula then joins that one fused unit, exactly as it joins `לִפְנֵי` → *was before* under rule 30, which states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of an expression does not defeat the condition. Test by the subtraction rules 16, 30 and 43 use: drop the copula and ask whether the preposition has lost a rendering of its own or only the clause has lost the tense English writes for it. Where only the clause is diminished, the preposition has no separate English and fuses; where an English preposition of its own remains — *is in their hands* — the first sentence of this rule governs and the copula stays with it. Do not reach for rule 2 to split the fused pair on the ground that the noun or name holds an English word of its own: that reasoning is rule 57's, where each of two nouns holds a word, and here the preposition holds none. The corpus reads `לְ` + the divine name this way in six units across five chapters — *is Jehovah's*, *shall be Jehovah's*, *am Jehovah's*, and a bare *Jehovah's* — and never splits a copula onto the preposition beside a separately aligned name. **And every sentence above governs a preposition that is itself the clause's predicate, never one heading an adjunct the ASV has merely placed the copula beside.** Where a nominal predicate stands in the verbless clause and a prepositional phrase modifies it, the copula and any dummy subject are rule 20's and join that nominal, whichever order the ASV writes the two in: `חֻקַּת עוֹלָם לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם` → *it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations* and `מֵאֵת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּרִית עוֹלָם` → *it is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting covenant* are one construction, and both give the copula to the construct nominal, the second unit discontinuous around the fronted phrase under rule 25 while the preposition keeps only the English written for its own relation. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, exactly as rule 20 directs, since a phrase the ASV fronts puts the copula beside something that predicates nothing; and do not let a fused compound preposition draw the copula in under rule 30's one-rendering condition, which reaches a copula the construction hands to that expression and not one another morpheme is there to take. Where the clause writes no nominal predicate at all, nothing competes and the first sentence of this rule governs as before.
amendments.why: NUM.2.10, 2.18 and 2.25 are verbless clauses whose predicate is a directional noun with a directive he — דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה רְאוּבֵן תֵּימָנָה → On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben — and rule 49 as written gives the copula to 'the preposition heading that phrase', which is not present. The gap forced a correction pass in all three verses, whose review notes reason from rule 49 by analogy rather than from its text. Rule 32 already makes the directive he its own aligned unit by rule 11 where the ASV writes a word for it, so the widening is entailed rather than new doctrine, but leaving rule 49 to say 'preposition' means the next chapter with a locative he predicate re-derives it or, more likely, follows the ASV's inversion and puts the copula on the fronted subject. The added text keeps the rule's existing limits reachable: it is placed above the closing adjunct paragraph so 'every sentence above' still binds it, it defers to rule 30 where the he and its noun fuse into one word, and it names the counter-case in this same chapter — 2.3, where a participial subject makes the nominal the predicate and the copula goes there instead — so the widening cannot be read as a standing preference for the locative. I returned it as an amendment rather than a new rule because a new one pointing back at 49 would leave 49's narrower sentence in place for whoever reads it first.

conventions: In the encampment formulas, which side of the verbless clause is the predicate decides where the construction-supplied copula goes, and the Hebrew decides that rather than the ASV's inversion (rules 20, 49). Where a participial phrase opens the clause — וְהַחֹנִים קֵדְמָה מִזְרָחָה דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה יְהוּדָה at 2.3, וְהַחֹנִים עָלָיו מַטֵּה X at 2.5, 2.12 and 2.27 — that phrase is the subject and the following nominal the predicate, so shall be joins דֶּגֶל or מַטֶּה and the עַל inside the subject phrase keeps only its own next unto. Where no participle stands and the definite construct chain opens the clause — דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה X <direction>ָה at 2.10, 2.18 and 2.25, וְעָלָיו מַטֵּה מְנַשֶּׁה at 2.20 — the construct chain is the subject and the locative is the predicate, so shall be joins the directive he or עַל and the nominal keeps only its own English.

In the census figures the construction-supplied copula joins the numeral that opens the ASV's figure, not the one that opens the Hebrew's: אַרְבָּעָה וַחֲמִשִּׁים אֶלֶף → were fifty and four thousand puts were on חֲמִשִּׁים (so at 2.4, 2.6, 2.8, 2.11, 2.13, 2.15, 2.19, 2.21, 2.23, 2.26, 2.28, 2.30), while מְאַת אֶלֶף heading the figure takes were a hundred (2.9, 2.16, 2.24, 2.31) and שֵׁשׁ takes were six at 2.32. The tens and units words are then matched to each other across the ASV's reordering under rule 25, including where the ASV recomputes the figure: אַרְבָּעָה וְשִׁבְעִים → threescore and fourteen at 2.4 gives fourteen to אַרְבָּעָה and threescore to שִׁבְעִים, the only partition the two numeral tokens allow.

The direction nouns קֵדֶם, תֵּימָן, יָם and צָפוֹן are rendered the east, south, west and north side (2.3, 2.10, 2.18, 2.25). Side is the ASV's supplied generic and the the is supplied, so both join the direction noun's own unit and the head stays on the direction word by rule 31's subtraction — the ASV writes no bare side for any of these words, so the noun is not a class noun realizing the lexeme. The directive he standing on them keeps whatever separate word the ASV writes for it, On or toward, under rule 32.

report: Read all 34 verses end to end and all 24 candidate lemma groups. No construction is analysed two ways without something in the source licensing the difference, so no patches.

The copula in the verbless encampment formulas is the one construction with two treatments. Where a participial phrase is the subject the copula joins the nominal predicate (2.3 on דֶּגֶל; 2.5, 2.12, 2.27 on מַטֶּה); where the definite construct chain is the subject the copula joins the locative predicate (2.10, 2.18, 2.25 on the directive he; 2.20 on עַל). That is a difference in the Hebrew clause, not in the analysis, and the three directive-he verses already carry correction notes recording it. Written into the conventions log.

The census figures are internally uniform: the construction-supplied copula lands on the numeral opening the ASV's figure (were fifty, were threescore, were a hundred, were six), never on the numeral opening the Hebrew's, and the tens and units words are matched across the ASV's reordering — including 2.4, where threescore and fourteen recomputes four and seventy. Every waw in every figure has an English and standing between the same two numerals, so nothing is in surplus under rule 42.

בְּתוֹךְ split at 2.17 (in the midst) and fused at 2.33 (among) is rule 30's one-English-rendering condition working as stated, not a split; each verse names the other. כַּאֲשֶׁר is fused to as at both 2.17 and 2.33, headed on the preposition.

The chapter's single added unit is the italic And opening 2.7. Verified against the parallel formulas: 2.7 is the only one whose Hebrew has no opening waw, while 2.14, 2.22 and 2.29 all write one and all take And. Correct under rule 14's closing sentence.

Article handling is consistent across the two participles: הַחֹנִים takes those that (2.3, 2.5, 2.12, 2.27) while הַפְּקֻדִים takes only that (2.9, 2.16, 2.24, 2.31), because כֹּל stands in those clauses and takes All; the anarthrous construct פְּקוּדֵי at 2.32 takes the whole supplied noun phrase under rule 46. Rule 46's own test — read whether an article morpheme is present — accounts for all three.

BSB: three disagreements, all prepositions the ASV leaves unrendered — the lamed of לֵאמֹר at 2.1 (rule 27), the לְ after סָבִיב at 2.2 (rule 40, which cites this construction by name), and the לָ of לָאַחֲרֹנָה at 2.31 (rule 40). Documented convention differences; none is a genuine error, and none should be changed to move the aggregate.

One amendment, to rule 49. That rule gives the verbless clause's copula to 'the preposition heading that phrase', and 2.10, 2.18 and 2.25 have no preposition: the predicate's relation is carried by a directive he. Widening rule 49 is preferred to a new rule, which would leave the narrower sentence in place for whoever reads it first. I did not promote the numeral-copula placement: the corroborating corpus is two units (EXO.6.16, EXO.6.18, both giving were a hundred to a מְאַת that stands last in the Hebrew and first in the English), which is too thin to bind every later chapter, so it is recorded as a convention instead.
